questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had morning vomiting, irritability and an unsteady walk for 6 weeks. Exam shows papilledema and truncal ataxia. MRI shows a mass that fills the fourth ventricle, arises from its floor and extends out through the lateral foramina. The lateral and third ventricles are enlarged. Microscopy shows uniform tumor cells arranged around blood vessels, with a clear zone of fine cell processes between the nuclei and each vessel wall. A few cells form small canal-like spaces. Which tumor is this?
questions.explanation: A tumor growing from the **floor of the fourth ventricle** in a young child, with **obstructive hydrocephalus** and cells lined up around vessels (**perivascular pseudorosettes**) plus true **ependymal rosettes** (canals), is an **ependymoma**. **Medulloblastoma** is the tempting choice because it is also a posterior fossa tumor of children that causes hydrocephalus. But it arises from the **vermis** (roof side) and shows sheets of small round blue cells with **Homer-Wright rosettes**, which form around neuropil, not around vessels.
questions.explanation_pt: Um tumor que cresce do **assoalho do quarto ventrículo** em uma criança pequena, com **hidrocefalia obstrutiva** e células alinhadas ao redor dos vasos (**pseudorrosetas perivasculares**), além de **rosetas ependimárias** verdadeiras (canais), é um **ependimoma**. O **meduloblastoma** é a escolha tentadora, porque também é um tumor de fossa posterior da infância que causa hidrocefalia. Mas ele surge do **vérmis** (lado do teto) e mostra camadas de pequenas células redondas e azuis com **rosetas de Homer-Wright**, que se formam ao redor de neurópilo, e não ao redor de vasos.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man has his first generalized seizure at work. He has had mild headaches for about a year but is otherwise well. CT shows a mass in the right frontal lobe with coarse calcifications and little surrounding edema. A biopsy shows sheets of uniform cells with round nuclei, each surrounded by a halo of clear cytoplasm. A network of thin, branching capillaries runs between the cells. There is no necrosis. Which molecular finding is most likely in this tumor?
choices: Loss of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22q
Loss of the VHL gene on chromosome 3p
questions.explanation: A slow-growing, **calcified frontal** tumor that presents with **seizures** in a middle-aged adult, with *fried egg* cells and *chicken-wire* capillaries, is an **oligodendroglioma**. By definition it carries an **IDH mutation** together with **whole-arm 1p/19q codeletion**. **EGFR amplification in an IDH-wild-type** tumor is the tempting answer, but that profile belongs to **glioblastoma**, which shows necrosis with pseudopalisading and usually occurs in older adults. **BRAF fusion** is typical of pilocytic astrocytoma, and NF2 loss is typical of meningioma and schwannoma.
questions.explanation_pt: Um tumor de crescimento lento, **frontal e calcificado**, que se apresenta com **crises epilépticas** em um adulto de meia-idade, com células em *fried egg* (ovo frito) e capilares em *chicken-wire* (tela de galinheiro), é um **oligodendroglioma**. Por definição, ele tem **mutação de IDH** junto com **codeleção 1p/19q** (de braços inteiros). A **amplificação de EGFR em tumor IDH tipo selvagem** é a resposta tentadora, mas esse perfil pertence ao **glioblastoma**, que mostra necrose com pseudopaliçada e geralmente ocorre em adultos mais velhos. A **fusão de BRAF** é típica do astrocitoma pilocítico, e a perda de NF2 é típica do meningioma e do schwannoma.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV infection stopped his antiretroviral therapy 1 year ago. He has had headache and low-grade fever for 10 days, and since yesterday his left arm feels weak. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Exam shows mild weakness of the left arm and no neck stiffness. Laboratory results: CD4+ count 45/µL (normal 500-1,500); serum anti-*Toxoplasma* IgG positive; serum cryptococcal antigen negative. MRI shows three ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema: one in the right basal ganglia and two at the gray-white junction of the frontal lobes. Which is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Restart antiretrovirals and repeat MRI in 6 months
questions.explanation: In a patient with a **CD4 count below 100/µL**, **multiple ring-enhancing lesions** (basal ganglia and gray-white junction) and **positive *Toxoplasma* IgG** point to **cerebral toxoplasmosis**, so the next step is **empiric treatment** with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine (with leucovorin to protect the marrow). Clinical and imaging improvement within about 2 to 3 weeks supports the diagnosis. **Brain biopsy** is the tempting choice, but it is kept for lesions that do not respond, or for a single lesion that suggests **primary CNS lymphoma** (for example with **EBV DNA** in the CSF). Amphotericin with flucytosine treats cryptococcal meningitis, which rarely causes ring-enhancing masses, and his antigen is negative.
questions.explanation_pt: Em um paciente com **CD4 abaixo de 100/µL**, **múltiplas lesões com realce em anel** (núcleos da base e junção entre substância cinzenta e branca) e **IgG anti-*Toxoplasma* positiva** indicam **neurotoxoplasmose**; por isso o próximo passo é o **tratamento empírico** com pirimetamina e sulfadiazina (com ácido folínico para proteger a medula óssea). A melhora clínica e de imagem em cerca de 2 a 3 semanas reforça o diagnóstico. A **biópsia cerebral** é a escolha tentadora, mas fica reservada para lesões que não respondem, ou para lesão única que sugere **linfoma primário do SNC** (por exemplo, com **DNA de EBV** no LCR). Anfotericina com flucitosina trata a meningite criptocócica, que raramente causa massas com realce em anel, e o antígeno dele é negativo.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man is the driver in a high-speed car crash. He is unconscious at the scene and never wakes up; there is no lucid interval. On arrival his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 6. Head CT shows no skull fracture, no extra-axial blood collection and no midline shift; only a few tiny hemorrhages are seen deep in the brain. Two days later he is still in a coma. MRI now shows many small lesions in the corpus callosum, the dorsolateral upper brainstem and at the gray-white junction. Which mechanism best explains his brain injury?
choices: Tearing of bridging veins between the cortex and the dural sinuses
Laceration of the middle meningeal artery
Impact of the brain on the skull opposite the site of the blow
Shearing of axons by rotational acceleration and deceleration
Rupture of a saccular aneurysm in the circle of Willis
questions.explanation: Immediate, lasting **coma** with a CT that looks **almost normal**, followed by MRI lesions in the **corpus callosum**, **dorsolateral brainstem** and **gray-white junction**, is **diffuse axonal injury**. Fast **rotational** acceleration and deceleration stretch and tear axons where tissues of different density meet; microscopy shows **axonal swellings** (*retraction balls*). **Contrecoup contusion** is the tempting choice, but contusions are surface bruises at the **frontal and temporal poles**, not scattered deep white-matter lesions. Bridging-vein and middle meningeal artery tears produce subdural and epidural hematomas, which CT would show.
questions.explanation_pt: **Coma** imediato e persistente com TC **quase normal**, seguido de lesões na RM no **corpo caloso**, no **tronco encefálico dorsolateral** e na **junção entre substância cinzenta e branca**, é **lesão axonal difusa**. Aceleração e desaceleração **rotacionais** rápidas estiram e rompem axônios onde se encontram tecidos de densidades diferentes; a microscopia mostra **tumefações axonais** (*retraction balls*, esferoides axonais). A **contusão por contragolpe** é a escolha tentadora, mas as contusões são lesões de superfície nos **polos frontais e temporais**, e não lesões espalhadas na substância branca profunda. A ruptura de veias-ponte e da artéria meníngea média produz hematomas subdural e epidural, que a TC mostraria.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a large glioblastoma in the right frontal lobe. Over 2 days she develops new weakness of the left leg. Her left arm, face and speech are normal, and both pupils are equal and react to light. CT shows the right frontal mass with marked edema. The right cingulate gyrus is pushed under the free edge of the falx cerebri toward the left side. Compression of which artery best explains her new deficit?
choices: Paramedian branches of the basilar artery
questions.explanation: The cingulate gyrus sliding under the falx is **subfalcine herniation**. It can press the **anterior cerebral artery** (its pericallosal branch) against the falx, causing ischemia of the medial frontal cortex, which holds the **leg** part of the motor strip, so the opposite leg becomes weak. The **middle cerebral artery** is the tempting choice, but its territory would weaken the face and arm more than the leg. The posterior cerebral artery and basilar branches are hit in **uncal** and downward herniation, which would also change the pupils.
questions.explanation_pt: O giro do cíngulo deslizando sob a foice é a **herniação subfalcina**. Ela pode comprimir a **artéria cerebral anterior** (seu ramo pericaloso) contra a foice, causando isquemia do córtex frontal medial, que contém a representação da **perna** no córtex motor; por isso a perna contralateral fica fraca. A **artéria cerebral média** é a escolha tentadora, mas seu território enfraqueceria mais a face e o braço do que a perna. A artéria cerebral posterior e os ramos da basilar são afetados na herniação **uncal** e descendente, que também alteraria as pupilas.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman takes prednisone every day for polymyalgia rheumatica. She has had fever and a severe headache for 1 day and is now drowsy. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), and she has neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture results: opening pressure 32 cm H2O (normal 10-20); white cells 1,800/µL with 90% neutrophils; glucose 28 mg/dL (serum glucose 110 mg/dL); protein 190 mg/dL. The Gram stain shows no organisms. Ceftriaxone and vancomycin are started. Which additional drug should be given, and for which organism?
questions.explanation: The CSF is **bacterial**: many **neutrophils**, a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of about **0.25** (28/110) and high protein. In a patient **over 50** or **immunosuppressed** (here chronic prednisone), *Listeria monocytogenes* must be covered, and it is **intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins**, so **ampicillin** is added. *Listeria* is often missed on Gram stain, so a negative stain does not exclude it. Fluconazole for *Cryptococcus* is the tempting choice in an immunosuppressed patient, but cryptococcal meningitis is subacute with a **lymphocytic** CSF, not an acute neutrophilic one.
questions.explanation_pt: O LCR é **bacteriano**: muitos **neutrófilos**, relação glicose LCR/sérica de cerca de **0,25** (28/110) e proteína alta. Em paciente **acima de 50 anos** ou **imunossuprimido** (aqui, prednisona crônica), é preciso cobrir *Listeria monocytogenes*, que tem **resistência intrínseca às cefalosporinas**; por isso se acrescenta **ampicilina**. A *Listeria* muitas vezes não aparece no Gram, então um Gram negativo não a exclui. Fluconazol para *Cryptococcus* é a escolha tentadora em imunossuprimido, mas a meningite criptocócica é subaguda e tem LCR **linfocítico**, e não neutrofílico agudo.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman from a rural area of Brazil has a focal seizure with jerking of her right hand, followed by a brief generalized seizure. She has been a strict vegetarian all her life and has never eaten pork. A relative who lives with her was recently treated for an intestinal tapeworm. CT shows several small cysts in both cerebral hemispheres; some contain a bright dot inside, and there are also a few small calcifications. Serum antibodies against *Taenia solium* are positive. How did she most likely acquire this infection?
choices: Ingesting eggs shed by a human tapeworm carrier
Eating undercooked pork that contained larval cysts
Ingesting oocysts passed in the feces of an infected cat
Swallowing eggs passed in the feces of an infected dog
Skin penetration by larvae while wading in fresh water
questions.explanation: Cysts with a central dot (the **scolex**) and calcified older lesions in a young adult with **seizures** are **neurocysticercosis**. It follows ingestion of *Taenia solium* **eggs**, which come from the stool of a **human carrier** of the adult worm (fecal-oral spread, often within a household), so a vegetarian can be infected. **Undercooked pork** is the tempting answer, but eating the larval cysts in meat gives only an **intestinal tapeworm** (taeniasis), not cysts in the brain. Eggs from dog feces (*Echinococcus*) usually form large hydatid cysts in the liver.
questions.explanation_pt: Cistos com um ponto central (o **escólex**) e lesões antigas calcificadas em um adulto jovem com **crises epilépticas** indicam **neurocisticercose**. Ela resulta da ingestão de **ovos** de *Taenia solium*, que vêm das fezes de um **portador humano** do verme adulto (transmissão fecal-oral, muitas vezes no mesmo domicílio); por isso uma vegetariana pode se infectar. A **carne de porco malcozida** é a resposta tentadora, mas comer os cisticercos da carne causa apenas a **teníase** intestinal, e não cistos no cérebro. Ovos de fezes de cães (*Echinococcus*) geralmente formam grandes cistos hidáticos no fígado.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had worsening hearing and ringing in both ears for 1 year. Her father became deaf in his 30s and had surgery for a brain tumor. Exam shows sensorineural hearing loss on both sides. Slit-lamp exam shows lens opacities, and she has only one small café-au-lait spot. MRI shows enhancing masses in both internal auditory canals that extend into the cerebellopontine angles, plus a dural-based mass over the left frontal convexity. A mutation in the gene that encodes which protein is most likely?
questions.explanation: **Bilateral vestibular schwannomas**, a **meningioma**, early **cataracts** and an affected parent (autosomal dominant) define **neurofibromatosis type 2**. The *NF2* gene on **chromosome 22** encodes **merlin** (schwannomin), a tumor suppressor that links the cell membrane to the cytoskeleton. **Neurofibromin** is the tempting choice, but **NF1** (chromosome 17) causes many café-au-lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, Lisch nodules and optic gliomas, not bilateral CN VIII tumors. Hamartin is lost in tuberous sclerosis, and menin in MEN1.
questions.explanation_pt: **Schwannomas vestibulares bilaterais**, um **meningioma**, **catarata** precoce e um genitor afetado (autossômica dominante) definem a **neurofibromatose tipo 2**. O gene *NF2*, no **cromossomo 22**, codifica a **merlina** (schwannomina), um supressor tumoral que liga a membrana celular ao citoesqueleto. A **neurofibromina** é a escolha tentadora, mas a **NF1** (cromossomo 17) causa muitas manchas café com leite, neurofibromas cutâneos, nódulos de Lisch e gliomas ópticos, e não tumores bilaterais do NC VIII. A hamartina é perdida na esclerose tuberosa, e a menina, na NEM1.
